claims.claim: The A-band is made up of approximately 500 parallel thick filaments per μm2 cross-sectional area that sit in register and are connected at the M-band through force-bearing M-bridges, predominately made up of myomesin.
claims.source: The A-band is made up of ~500 parallel thick filaments per μm2 cross-sectional area that sit in register and are connected at the M-band through force-bearing M-bridges, predominately made up of myomesin (Lange et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the structural description.

claims.claim: At rest, all thick filaments are radially and longitudinally centered in a sarcomere by titin-based forces.
claims.source: At rest, all thick filaments are radially and longitudinally centered in a sarcomere by titin-based forces (Horowits, 1999), and so tension on the M-band structures, caused by adjacent thick filaments, is ~0 pN.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: Thin filament length variability can be as large as 100 nm.
claims.source: Importantly, because of thin filament length variability as large as 100 nm (Littlefield and Fowler, 2002), the force producing region between each half-thick filament and thin filament is variable at the immediate onset of contraction.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: M-band structures can extend up to 70 nm at low force.
claims.source: Thick-filament movement away from a central position is exacerbated by M-band structures, which can extend up to 70 nm at low force (Berkemeier et al., 2011; Xiao and Gräter, 2014), allowing thick-filament movement toward the stronger side of the sarcomere during active contraction and enhancing force imbalances especially during prolonged contractions.
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Forces on M-bridges are conservatively estimated to be <50 pN (0–6.25% maximal force at optimal overlap, P0) on average, with pockets that could reach as high as 120 pN (~25% P0) at 2.6–2.7 µm SL.
claims.source: Considering this within the context of sarcomere geometry, filament overlap, and structural mechanics between thick filaments, we conservatively estimate forces on M-bridges are <50 pN (0–6.25% maximal force at optimal overlap, P0) on average, with pockets that could reach as high as 120 pN (~25% P0) at 2.6–2.7 µm SL.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on sarcomere mechanics.

claims.claim: There are six titin filaments per half-thick filament.
claims.source: On the other side of the equation, there are the six titin filaments per half-thick filament (Liversage et al., 2001), and their forces have been estimated from passive myofibril mechanics (Linke et al., 1998b).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claims.claim: Thick-filament movement within A-bands will lead to a titin length change of approximately 35 nm and generate a titin-based centering force in psoas of approximately 12 pN/molecule at 2.65 μm SL.
claims.source: Thick-filament movement within A-bands will lead to a titin length change of ~35 nm (six lengthening on one side/six shortening on the other side) and generate a titin-based centering force in psoas of ~12 pN/molecule at 2.65 μm SL (Linke et al., 1998b; Prado et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the calculation.

claims.claim: Titin-based centering forces are up to an order of magnitude smaller than potential thick-filament movement forces.
claims.source: Based on this first approximation, titin-based centering forces are up to an order of magnitude smaller than potential thick-filament movement forces.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the force calculations.

claims.claim: To produce 120 pN of centering force and provide A-band stability, active titin stiffness would need to be approximately 4x larger than measured in passive muscle.
claims.source: To produce 120 pN of centering force against our upper estimate of thick filament force, and provide A-band stability, active titin stiffness would need to be approximately 4x larger than measured in passive muscle.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on the force requirements.

claims.claim: Recent hypotheses in muscle contraction purport that titin undergoes a structural rearrangement during contraction that leads to actin binding at or around the N2A/PEVK regions upon activation.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent hypotheses in muscle contraction purport that titin undergoes a structural rearrangement during contraction that leads to actin binding at or around the N2A/PEVK regions upon activation (Dutta et al., 2018; Kulke et al., 2001; Nagy et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claims.claim: The functional extensibility of I-band titin is thought to change so that only the stiffer PEVK region, and not the more compliant proximal Ig region, is extensible during contraction.
claims.source: Consequently, the functional extensibility of I-band titin is thought to change so that only the stiffer PEVK region, and not the more compliant proximal Ig region, is extensible (Linke, 2018; Nishikawa, 2020; Powers et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claims.claim: The structural change of titin during contraction has the effect of increasing titin stiffness by fourfold to sixfold.
claims.source: This structural change has the effect of increasing titin stiffness by fourfold to sixfold (Nishikawa, 2020), which is in agreement with our estimation that titin must become up to fourfold stiffer in active, compared to passive, permeabilized fibers.
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation and compared to the calculations in the current study.

claims.claim: The atomic structure of the thick filament remains to be fully resolved in mammalian muscles.
claims.source: The atomic structure of the thick filament remains to be fully resolved in mammalian muscles (Irving, 2017; Zoghbi et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: The central portion of the thick filament contains an even volume of myosin proteins, whereas the last approximately 160 nm of the thick-filament ends (including the D-zone) taper down until only a few myosin proteins are left.
claims.source: However, we do know that the central portion of the thick filament contains an even volume of myosin proteins, whereas the last ~160 nm of the thick-filament ends (including the D-zone; Figure 8) taper down until only a few myosin proteins are left, in a potentially unstabilized manner.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about thick filament structure.

claims.claim: The six titin filaments that run along the half-thick filament all converge at the end of the thick filament into the end-filament.
claims.source: Because the six titin filaments that run along the half-thick filament all converge at the end of the thick filament into the end-filament (Houmeida et al., 2008), it is not difficult to consider that this region of titin can help stabilize the tips of the thick filaments (Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the structural description.

claims.claim: The end-filament region of titin can help stabilize the tips of the thick filaments.
claims.source: Because the six titin filaments that run along the half-thick filament all converge at the end of the thick filament into the end-filament (Houmeida et al., 2008), it is not difficult to consider that this region of titin can help stabilize the tips of the thick filaments (Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to support the hypothesis.

claims.claim: In zebrafish containing an A-band titin null mutation, prenatal sarcomeres assemble normally, but quickly degrade at the start of prenatal contractile activity.
claims.source: This view is supported by the findings in zebrafish containing an A-band titin null mutation, where prenatal sarcomeres assemble normally, but quickly degrade at the start of prenatal contractile activity, indicating a lack of structural stability and a need for titin proteins for stabilization (Myhre et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

results.result: The HaloTag-TEV mouse model allows graded titin cleavage with Het fibers containing approximately 50% HaloTag-TEV titins that are effectively cleaved by TEV protease, while Hom fibers contain 100% cleavable titin.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C42 collectively establish the TC mouse model and demonstrate graded titin cleavage. Multiple independent quantification methods (IF, IEM, gel electrophoresis, western blot) converge on ~50% mutant titin in Het fibers (C36-C42), and the model does not affect baseline muscle function (C35). The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: Passive longitudinal forces scale linearly with the proportion of intact titin springs, with titin contributing 50-55% of passive force in permeabilized fibers at physiological sarcomere lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C47 and C89, C99-C100 demonstrate dose-dependent passive force reduction with titin cleavage. The linear relationship is supported by strong correlations (R²>0.5) at moderate-to-long SLs (C46), appropriate controls, and consistency across elastic and viscous components (C44). The ~50% residual force in Hom fibers (C100) is appropriately attributed to non-titin structures.

results.result: Titin contributes approximately one-third of transverse (radial compressive) stiffness in permeabilized skeletal fibers, which is relatively less than its contribution to longitudinal forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 and C109 demonstrate a ~33% decrease in both indentation depth and Young's modulus after titin cleavage in Hom fibers using AFM. The conclusion that transverse stiffness depends less on titin than longitudinal stiffness (C54, C109) is supported by comparing these data to the passive stretch results. Appropriate controls and sufficient sample sizes strengthen the finding.

results.result: Under sustained mechanical stretch, titin cleavage causes progressive Z-disk misalignment and disorder, demonstrating titin's role in maintaining Z-disk organization under mechanical stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C62 and C91 show time-resolved force decreases (C55-C58) and corresponding ultrastructural changes (C59-C61) with graded severity from Het to Hom. The custom 'fracture area' metric quantifies Z-disk disorder (C60-C61), and the conclusion about titin's role in balancing I-bands (C62) is well-supported by the dose-dependent relationship. The kinetics data (C56) appropriately establish the timecourse.

results.result: Cleaved titin recoils toward the Z-disk but is prevented from full recoil by interactions with thin filaments; removal of actin allows complete titin recoil.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 demonstrate partial titin recoil using multiple antibodies at different I-band positions, with bimodal distributions in Het fibers (C65) and incomplete recoil in Hom (C66). The gelsolin experiments (C68-C69) provide strong mechanistic evidence that actin removal permits full recoil. The conclusion about titin-actin interactions (C70, C92, C113) is well-supported by the experimental design and consistent with cited literature.

results.result: Titin cleavage reduces active contractile force in a dose-dependent manner (23% in Het, 46% in Hom), demonstrating that titin-based forces are crucial for maintaining high active force levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73, C93, and C118 show graded active force reduction with titin cleavage using appropriate before/after comparisons at physiological SL (2.6 μm). The dose-dependent relationship and statistical significance support the conclusion. This is stated as a novel finding (C118) that directly addresses the study's main question about titin's role in active contraction.

results.result: During active contraction with cleaved titin, A-bands undergo severe disruption including thick filament separation, movement toward Z-disks, M-band disorganization, and myosin shedding from filament tips.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C88 and C94-C96 describe progressive A-band disruption using multiple complementary approaches (EM, IF with HaloTag and myomesin markers). The observations of thick filament movement (C76, C86), shortening (C77, C82), M-band broadening (C83-C85), and the conclusion about titin's protective role (C88, C96) are well-documented with appropriate imaging evidence. The graded severity from Het to Hom supports causality.

results.result: After titin cleavage and active contraction, the MyHC/NEB ratio shows a reduction trend (p=0.081 for Wt vs Hom), suggesting myosin molecules float out of the sarcomere.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 report protein ratio changes using loose gels, but the authors acknowledge 'substantial data scatter' (C78) and the key MyHC/NEB comparison is not statistically significant (p=0.081, C80). While the trend supports the myosin shedding hypothesis (C81), the high variability and marginal statistics make this result uncertain. Additional replicates or alternative quantification methods would strengthen this finding.

results.result: In Hom fibers held at long length, titin cleavage causes an over-proportionate ~67% decrease in passive force, potentially explained by coordinated retraction of the six-titin end-filament as a unit.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 reports the over-proportionate force decrease, but the mechanistic explanation (C105) is speculative ('may retract as a unit'). While the structural context about the end-filament is well-cited (C102-C104), the proposed mechanism lacks direct experimental evidence. The observation is interesting but the interpretation remains uncertain without additional validation.

results.result: To buffer forces during contraction, titin stiffness must increase approximately 4-fold, consistent with hypotheses that titin undergoes activation-dependent structural changes involving enhanced actin binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 present force calculations estimating that titin-based centering forces (~12 pN/molecule) are an order of magnitude smaller than thick-filament movement forces (up to 120 pN), requiring ~4x stiffness increase (C128). This calculation is consistent with cited hypotheses about activation-dependent titin-actin binding (C129-C131) that would increase stiffness 4-6 fold. While the calculations involve assumptions, they are reasonable and well-explained, supporting the main conclusions (C11-C12).

results.result: Background: Titin is a major contributor to passive force, but its role in active force generation has been unresolved despite being critical for sarcomeric function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C13-C24 establish the scientific context with appropriate citations. The historical perspective (C13-C14), titin's established role in passive force (C1, C21-C22), and the knowledge gap regarding active contraction (C2, C23) are well-documented. This provides clear justification for the study.

results.result: Background: Previous approaches to study titin's role in contraction have limitations including muscle dystrophy phenotypes in genetic models and non-specific protein degradation in biochemical methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 document limitations of prior approaches with appropriate citations, providing clear rationale for the TC mouse model. The critique of previous methods (C30-C31) is fair and well-supported, establishing the need for the specific, controllable titin cleavage approach used in this study.

results.result: The study refines estimates of titin's contribution to passive force, showing it contributes 50-70% of longitudinal force in the physiological range, compared to previous estimates of >90% using high-salt extraction methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 and C106-C108 appropriately contextualize the findings relative to prior work. The comparison to high-salt extraction methods (C106) and acknowledgment of their limitations (C107) strengthens the interpretation. The refined estimate (C108) is well-supported by the experimental data and represents an important update to the field.

results.result: Other cytoskeletal structures (microtubules, desmin, microfilaments) may contribute to transverse stiffness, and their contributions may be greater in intact fibers than in glycerol-permeabilized preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 appropriately acknowledge other contributors to cellular stiffness with citations and recognize methodological limitations of the permeabilization approach. This demonstrates appropriate scientific caution and suggests directions for future work.

results.result: Although titin-based passive forces are not detectable below 2.5 μm SL, the recoil data demonstrate that titin must generate some force at shorter sarcomere lengths down to ~1.8 μm.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 make a logical inference from the recoil experiments with appropriate citations to prior work. The reasoning that complete recoil to the Z-disk implies force generation even at short SLs is sound, though the magnitude of these forces remains unquantified. This represents a valid insight from the experimental observations.

results.result: Background: Titin has long been hypothesized to maintain A-band stability through centering forces, with structural context provided by thick filament organization and M-band connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C123 establish the historical context and structural framework with appropriate citations. The background on titin's proposed centering role (C116-C117, C119) and sarcomere architecture (C120-C123) provides necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: The end-filament region of titin may help stabilize thick filament tips, supported by observations in zebrafish titin null mutants where sarcomeres degrade upon contractile activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 discuss thick filament structure and propose a stabilization role for the titin end-filament with appropriate citations. The zebrafish data (C136) provides supporting evidence, though the mechanism remains incompletely resolved (C132). The speculation is reasonable and appropriately qualified.
